newsitem.title: USA: US House panel chides MMS on oil royalties losses.
newsitem.headline: US House panel chides MMS on oil royalties losses.

text.p: The U.S. treasury may have been shorted up to $2 billion in royalties underpaid by companies for extracting oil from federal lands, according to a House panel's report released Tuesday.

In a report to be considered by the House Government Oversight Committee later Tuesday, the panel chided the Interior Department's Minerals Management Service, the agency responsible for collecting royalties, for lagging in collecting underpaid amounts which may go back to 1978.

The panel also said the MMS must prepare a timetable for collecting payments, and immediately determine if underpayments occurred in states beside California, where the undervaluation issue has been fought in courts for years.
Royalties were based on prices posted by oil companies, which critics have said were set below market value.

The panel said its estimate of potential losses was based on the high-range estimate of an Interior Department official who said undervaluation of oil from federal lands, not including California, may be as much as 10 percent
The panel said that could amount to $1.3 billion, and combined that with the top-range estimate of an administration task force which said California losses could reach $856 million.
The MMS has disputed the high range estimate for California, and said it would go after some $440 million in royalties it said were underpaid from federal lands there.
The House panel's report said royalty underpayment was a "serious problem" that MMS has "failed to seriously address," and suggested MMS get outside audit assistance.
It also said the MMS should review its existing global settlements with oil companies that are intended to resolve a range of issues, but critics said reduced the potential for royalty collections.
"Global settlements between the federal government and major oil companies have not protected U.S. financial interests," the report said.
The MMS also should review royalty in-kind payments to see whether those also were undervalued, and should see that prices are not distorted on oil in pipelines that cross federal lands.

The subcommittee report came after the Interior Department's inspector general said in nine out of ten settlements reviewed, the settlements lacked some documentation and did not give reasons why the government reduced the amount of royalties it thought it was owed.
In one case, the department's watchdog said it found an unexplained $360 million gap between the MMS's estimate of the value of a disputed issue and the settlement.
The inspector general's draft report was was released last month by the Project on Government Oversight, and a final report was pending.
The MMS in the draft report said it was too tightly staffed to fully document their reasons for accepting lower royalties.
